item.title: Judge Clears New York City Rent Freeze Backed by Mayor Mamdani
item.description: A rent freeze backed by New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s administration was cleared by a state judge who dismissed a lawsuit filed by a group of landlords seeking to void the measure, which went into effect last month.
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: (Bloomberg) -- A rent freeze backed by New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s administration was cleared by a state judge who dismissed a lawsuit filed by a group of landlords seeking to void the measure, which went into effect last month.The landlords sued the city’s Rent Guidelines Board in July, arguing that Mamdani improperly influenced the vote and ignored evidence of rising operating costs for building owners. A judge on Wednesday threw out the case, saying the decision to implement the freeze was not “unreasonable, arbitrary or capricious” and must be upheld.But the judge, Brendan T. Lantry, sharply criticized Mamdani’s campaign promises to freeze the rent. The mayor’s comments were “reckless and irresponsible” because only the board can raise, freeze or adjust the rent of stabilized units in the city, the judge wrote. Correspondence between the mayor’s office and the board about the measure was “troubling” and “puts a dark shadow over the purported ‘independence’ of the board,” but it doesn’t show that the mayor dictated the decision, Lantry said.“The court recognizes that political candidates routinely comment on prevalent policy issues while running for an elected position, but to guarantee a rent freeze to millions of New Yorkers without the authority to do so, is irresponsible and, quite frankly, invited” the lawsuit, the judge wrote. Still, there is “nothing to suggest the guideline-setting process was an orchestrated ‘sham process,” Lantry said.In a statement, Mamdani cheered the decision. “This is a victory for tenants, for affordability and for the principle that working New Yorkers deserve a city they can afford to live in,” he said. “Because housing is not a luxury. It is a basic necessity. This holiday weekend, more than two million New Yorkers can breathe a little easier.”Randy Mastro, a lawyer for the landlords and a former deputy mayor in the Giuliani administration who has also challenged the pied-a-terre tax backed by Mamdani, didn’t respond to a message seeking comment.The suit came weeks after the board voted for the first time ever to freeze rents for both one-year and two-year leases for roughly 1 million stabilized apartments. The last one-year rent freeze was during the pandemic in 2020.Courts have historically deferred to the Rent Guidelines Board. A state court judge dismissed a challenge by landlords to a 2016 rent freeze. While that lawsuit claimed the board didn’t account for finances of the building, this challenge focused on the mayor’s involvement. Mamdani made the freeze a centerpiece of his mayoral campaign, contending that tenants squeezed by years of rising housing costs needed immediate relief. After taking office, he appointed a majority of the board’s members. A member of the board who represented landlords, Christina Smyth, resigned in protest hours before the vote. Tenant advocates hailed the vote as a long-overdue reset after inflation and housing shortages left many renters facing mounting financial pressure. Landlord and housing industry groups have warned that the freeze will make it harder for owners to maintain aging buildings and finance fixes as insurance, taxes and repair costs have surged amid a tight rental market.The case is Kenilworth Holdings LLC v New York City Rent Guidelines Board, 453580/2026, New York State Supreme Court, New York County.--With assistance from Laura Nahmias.More stories like this are available on bloomberg.com©2026 Bloomberg L.P.

item.title: San Francisco Coastline Is Swamped by Record-High King Tides
item.description: Record flooding from king tides is inundating the California coast Wednesday, compounded by a Pacific storm that’s contributing to flight delays in San Francisco.
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: (Bloomberg) -- Record flooding from king tides is inundating the California coast Wednesday, compounded by a Pacific storm that’s contributing to flight delays in San Francisco.Tuesday’s high tide of 8.23 feet (2.51 meters) was the largest ever recorded in the city during the month of November. Wednesday’s high tide may surpass it, said Sebastian Westerink, a US National Weather Service meteorologist in Monterey.“Today and tomorrow around noon are going to be the worst,” Westerink said. “Then it is going to start lowering from there.”About 145 flights through San Francisco International Airport were delayed Wednesday, according to FlightAware, a tracking site.Flood warnings remain across San Francisco, much of the Bay Area and the Pacific coastline. Gauges on Wednesday in Santa Barbara and San Diego recorded their highest tides ever, the weather service said, breaking records set about a month ago.Rough seas and dangerous swells have been spotted along California’s shores. Authorities in Marin County north of San Francisco issued a “shelter-in-place” order to residents in the Calles area of Stinson Beach as waves push past the beach. There’s also an evacuation warning in Stinson Beach — a community of 541 people — as large waves are expected through 2 p.m. local time.Evacuation warnings are in effect more than 300 miles (483 km) south in Ventura County. The alerts encompass waterfront neighborhoods recently fortified with protective berms.California’s king tides, the highest predicted tides of the year, recur when the sun, moon and Earth align and the moon is closest to Earth. This year, they’re arriving after El Niño helped raise sea levels and powerful waves battered the state’s coastline, damaging roads and destroying homes.Travel has become dangerous at times: King tides have forced road closures and shut down portions of the Pacific Coast Highway in Orange County, south of Los Angeles.--With assistance from Todd Woody.(Updates with flight delays in 4th paragraph. An earlier version corrected a detail involving Stinson Beach evacuation warning.)More stories like this are available on bloomberg.com©2026 Bloomberg L.P.

item.title: Abrego Garcia Can ‘Breathe Freely’ After He Arrives in Spain
item.description: Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the Salvadoran man deported to a notorious prison in El Salvador in what US officials called an “administrative error,” said he “can breathe freely” after arriving to Spain.
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: (Bloomberg) -- Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the Salvadoran man deported to a notorious prison in El Salvador in what US officials called an “administrative error,” said he “can breathe freely” after arriving to Spain.“Today we celebrate because I not only feel victorious and we won the fight,” Abrego Garcia said at press conference Wednesday. “This time because I’m leaving with my freedom, not like before when they took me out inhumanely.”Abrego Garcia’s battle was one of several high-profile legal disputes over the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. He was mistakenly deported last year to CECOT, a notorious Salvadoran mega-prison, only to be brought back to face criminal charges after the US Supreme Court ordered the government to facilitate his return to the US.He arrived in Madrid Wednesday after the 18-month legal battle where the government had sought to deport him to African countries, including Liberia. He had also faced a US human smuggling prosecution until a US judge in May dismissed the charges, concluding the government brought the case in retaliation for his fight against deportation.“We are going to continue to fight for all the people that are experiencing an injustice,” Abrego Garcia said. “Clearly the government did not decide where my story continues. My family and I decide where my story goes from here.”In 2019, an immigration court issued an order prohibiting the government from removing him to El Salvador after the court found he faced danger from a gang that had targeted his family.Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, his American attorney, said Wednesday that Abrego Garcia traveled to Spain under a tourist visa for a “short term” stay. The US government was required by court order to lift “all impediments” that barred Abrego Garcia from leaving the country, including removing him from a no-fly list.Abrego Garcia, whose wife and son are American citizens, could be eligible to return to the US as a legal permanent resident. But, he will need waivers from the State Department, which Secretary of State Marco Rubio will not grant, Sandoval-Moshenberg said. “It is going to be up to the next administration to reunite this family as quickly as possible,” he said. Senator Chris Van Hollen, a Democrat from Maryland who met with Abrego Garcia in the Salvadoran prison last year, said the Trump administration had engaged in a “vendetta” against him.“Kilmar and his family are relieved that he is now in a place of his choosing, a free man and living with dignity,” Van Hollen said. “I think the message for all of us is that it’s never wrong to stand up for our Constitution. It’s never wrong to stand up for the rule of law.”Both immigration advocates and the Trump administration said that Abrego Garcia’s departure was a win. Ama Frimpong, chief of services and legal advocacy at We Are CASA, said rather than being deported, Abrego Garcia made the “choice” in where he went.“This is what we fight form the freedom to choose how we live with safety and dignity,” she said.Meanwhile, DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin issued a statement taking credit for Abrego Garcia’s exit. He labeled Abrego Garcia as a “human trafficker” and “MS-13 gang member.”Abrego Garcia has denied the government’s allegations.More stories like this are available on bloomberg.com©2026 Bloomberg L.P.

item.title: Petrol and diesel prices today, November 25: Check fuel cost in Delhi, Mumbai, Bengaluru
item.description: Global oil prices steadied as traders balanced indications of rising global supply against escalating attacks on vessels near the Strait of Hormuz, Bloomberg reported.
item.dc:creator: Livemint
item.content:encoded: Petrol and diesel prices today, November 25: Petrol and diesel prices have remained largely steady across major cities despite a surge in global crude oil costs due to the US-Iran war, which led to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.Union Petroleum and Natural Gas Minister Hardeep Singh Puri attributed this to the Centre's strategy of cutting excise duties and managing domestic fuel supplies.Here is a look at the petrol and diesel prices in major metropolitan cities as of November 25:New Delhi: Petrol is retailing at ₹102.12 per litre, while diesel is priced at ₹95.20 per litre. The national capital continues to have relatively lower fuel prices compared to other metros.Mumbai: In the financial capital, petrol is priced at ₹111.21 per litre, and diesel costs ₹97.83 per litre.Chennai: Residents in Chennai are paying ₹107.76 per litre for petrol and ₹99.55 per litre for diesel.Kolkata: Petrol costs ₹113.51 per litre, while diesel costs ₹99.82 per litre.Bengaluru: Petrol is priced at ₹110.44 per litre, and diesel at ₹99.56 per litre.Hyderabad: Petrol costs ₹116.15 per litre, while diesel costs ₹104.23 per litre.Petrol and diesel prices in other metro cities today Source: GoodReturnsOil steady after gainOil prices steadied as traders balanced indications of rising global supply against escalating attacks on vessels near the Strait of Hormuz, Bloomberg reported.Brent crude traded around $91 a barrel after climbing 2.3% in the previous session, while West Texas Intermediate (WTI) hovered below $82. On Tuesday, Iran claimed a fourth tanker was struck by a mine, according to the Fars news agency, extending a recent wave of vessel attacks by the Islamic Republic.Tehran also warned it would tighten its grip over the Strait of Hormuz until its demands are met, Tasnim reported—highlighting that an end to the nearly nine-month conflict remains out of reach. Even so, crude shipments from the Persian Gulf have surged in recent months, prompting the International Energy Agency (IEA) to forecast that the market will tip into a surplus this quarter.“The reality on the ground is more a ‘war but no war’ situation, with spasms of violence,” Robert Yawger, director of the energy futures division at Mizuho Securities USA LLC, told Bloomberg. Under that scenario, “look for the supply surplus to become the dominant theme in coming weeks,” he added.Brent has dropped sharply this month as Gulf exports climbed and US President Donald Trump held off on renewed strikes against Iran following the US midterm elections.Adding to the downward pressure, a key timespread for the Middle East’s Dubai crude benchmark flipped into a bearish structure this week, signalling that supply is now outpacing demand, Bloomberg noted.
